summary: The Intermediate Flow Selection Process picks a subset of observed flows, and can sit at an IPFIX Exporter, Collector, or Mediator. It reduces the effort of post-processing and transferring flow records. This document describes the motivations and techniques for it.

eli5.summary: Keeping every record can be too much work. This explains ways to pick just some records to keep.

subtitle: Ways for an IPFIX device to keep only some of the traffic flows it sees, and how to describe and report that choice.

tldr.problem: Capturing, storing, exporting and analysing every flow record can cost too many resources, and some applications only care about certain flows.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7014 defines the Intermediate Flow Selection Process, which takes flow records in and passes a subset on, using filtering, sampling or flow-state dependent methods. It also defines the parameters to configure these methods and new IPFIX Information Elements to report what was selected.
tldr.outcome: A collector can tell how many flows were observed and how many were selected, which is needed to judge how accurate any estimate is. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7014 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2013. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it builds on RFC 7011, the IPFIX protocol.

sections.title: Why Select Flows at All
sections.content:
A Flow is a set of packets with common properties, as defined in RFC 7011. An Intermediate Flow Selection Process takes Flow Records as input and selects a subset of them as output. It can limit the resources needed to capture, store, export and post-process Flow Records, and it can pick out the particular flows an application cares about.

The RFC categorises the techniques and describes configuration and reporting parameters for them. It also covers parameters for flow-state dependent packet selection from RFC 5475, even though that is technically packet selection, because it is often used to cut the resources needed for flow capture and was only briefly discussed there.
sections.eli5: Keeping every single record is like keeping every receipt you ever got. Sometimes it is smarter to keep just the ones you need.

sections.title: Flow Selection Versus Packet Selection
sections.content:
Packet selection treats packets as the basic element. Flow selection treats whole Flows as the basic element and works on Complete Flows: after selection, either all packets of a flow are kept or all are discarded. Flow selection normally happens after Packet Classification, because that step decides which flow a packet belongs to. It can also run before classification, but then it can only use the Flow Key (or a hash of it), not things like flow size or duration.

Some techniques are hard to place. Property Match Filtering on a destination address can count as both, if flows are defined by destination address. Flow-state dependent packet selection, such as Sample and Hold, Fast Filtered Sampling and Sticky Sampling, favours packets of large flows but does not guarantee complete flows, so strictly speaking it is packet selection.

The RFC also separates the process from the Intermediate Selection Process of RFC 6183. That one evaluates only Flow Record values. The Intermediate Flow Selection Process can also use Flow Selection State, such as Flow Cache occupancy or export link capacity.
sections.eli5: Picking packets is like grabbing single pages from a pile of books. Picking flows is like grabbing whole books: you either take the entire book or leave it.

sections.title: Where the Process Sits in IPFIX
sections.content:
The process can be deployed in three places: in the Metering Process at an IPFIX Exporter, in the Exporting Process at a Collector, or inside an IPFIX Mediator.

  • Metering Process: selection before Packet Classification relies on the Flow Key and cannot use flow size or duration. It reduces resources for every later stage, or picks flows whose characteristics are visible per packet, such as flows to specific IP addresses.
  • Exporting Process: selection works on Flow Records, so it can use flow size and duration. It can export only the records of interest, or only as many as the available resources, such as limited export link capacity, can handle.
  • Mediator: it takes a Flow Record stream as input and can also correlate data from different Exporters, for example by selecting only flows that were recorded on two or more Exporters.
sections.eli5: You can sort the mail at the post office where it is collected, while it is being sent on, or at a middle sorting depot. Each spot can use different clues.

sections.title: The Selection Techniques
sections.content:
A technique must select either all or none of a flow's packets, otherwise it counts as packet selection. The RFC splits the techniques into filtering, sampling and flow-state dependent methods. To be IPFIX compliant, at least one of the Flow Filtering schemes MUST be implemented.

Flow Filtering is a deterministic function. Property Match Filtering selects flows whose Flow Key, timestamp or per-flow counter matches a value, a set of values or an interval, for example flows above a threshold number of octets. Hash-based Flow Filtering maps the Flow Key through a hash function onto a range and selects the flow if the hash falls in a chosen Hash Selection Range. It can emulate random sampling while still letting different Observation Points select the same flows; for that, the Hash Domain MUST only include parts of the Flow Record that do not change along the flow path.

Flow Sampling uses record order or arrival time. Systematic sampling picks, for example, every N-th flow, or flows seen between time-based start and stop triggers. Random sampling is either n-out-of-N, where n flows are drawn from a population of N, or probabilistic, where each flow is chosen with a given probability. That probability may differ per flow, for example favouring large-volume flows.

Flow-state dependent selection decides using per-flow state kept in the Flow Cache. Two algorithms are described. The Frequent algorithm aims to find flows above a 1/k fraction of the packet stream using a Flow Cache of size k-1 with a counter per flow. Lossy counting splits the packet stream into windows of size N=1/e and decrements all counters at the end of each window.
sections.eli5: You can keep only the kids wearing red hats (filtering), every fifth kid in line (systematic sampling), or flip a coin for each kid (random sampling). You can also keep the kids who keep showing up a lot.

sections.title: Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
Each technique needs its own settings, and the RFC lists them as the basis for an information model for configuring the process on an IPFIX device. Property Match Filtering needs the Information Element to test and a Selection Value or Value Interval.

Hash-based Flow Filtering needs a Hash Domain, a Hash Function (BOB, IP Shift-XOR (IPSX) or CRC-32 are named), a Hash Selection Range and optionally a random seed or initializer value. Flow-state dependent selection uses a frequency threshold s and an accuracy parameter e.

Systematic time-based sampling uses an interval length and a spacing, both in microseconds. Count-based sampling uses an interval length and a spacing in numbers of flows. Random n-out-of-N sampling uses the population size N and the sampling size n, and probabilistic sampling uses a sampling probability p. Flow-state dependent packet selection uses packet selection probabilities per flow-state interval, plus extras such as packet size.
sections.eli5: Every picking method has knobs to turn, like how many to skip or how likely each one is to be chosen. This part lists the knobs.

sections.title: Reporting and New Information Elements
sections.content:
The process MUST export Information Elements that say how many packets and flows were observed and how many were selected. This lets a receiver compute the Attained Selection Fraction from RFC 5476, which matters for stating accuracy. The number of dropped elements can be derived from these totals.

IANA registered new Information Elements, among them flowSelectorAlgorithm (ID 390), flowSelectedOctetDeltaCount (391), flowSelectedPacketDeltaCount (392), flowSelectedFlowDeltaCount (393), selectorIDTotalFlowsObserved (394), selectorIDTotalFlowsSelected (395), samplingFlowInterval (396), samplingFlowSpacing (397), flowSamplingTimeInterval (398), flowSamplingTimeSpacing (399) and hashFlowDomain (400).

The flowSelectorAlgorithm element carries a technique identifier, 1 to 9 as shown below. New identifiers are assigned First Come First Served with Expert Review, and experts should check a request against the policies in RFC 2804. The RFC also registers an object identifier, number 8, in the IPFIX-SELECTOR-MIB functions subregistry.
sections.eli5: When you pick some records, you also write a note saying how many you looked at and how many you kept, so others can trust your results.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Flow data can be sensitive for privacy reasons and needs protection; the privacy considerations of RFC 7011 apply. Sampling and hash-based filtering aim to give a representative subset, so an adversary may try to steer which flows are selected, for example to dodge accounting or hide attack traffic. For time-based systematic sampling, an attacker could learn the start and stop triggers by sending test packets. For hash-based selection, the hash function discussion in Section 6.2.3 of RFC 5475 applies.

The protocol that configures or reports selection parameters is out of scope, but the RFC states initial requirements for it: protect configuration information from disclosure (encryption), from modification (authentication for integrity), and from being sent by unauthorised nodes (access control lists and source authentication). A fuller threat assessment is needed once a specific protocol is proposed.
sections.eli5: If a sneaky person learns your picking rule, they can arrange to never be picked. So the rule and its settings should be kept private and not tampered with.
